Due on Wednesday, November 4th.

### Part 1
(40 points)

This exercise is basically just like [Part 1](../applicative_cg/assignment.html#part-1) of [the previous assignment](../applicative_cg/assignment.html).
I want you to have a chance to practice a bit more figuring out what syntactic category and semantic type something has, based on a description of its distribution.
Importantly, none of the expression behaviors I will describe here necessarily correspond to anything you actually see in English or any other language.
The point of the exercise is for you to get comfortable translating the informal description in English into a formal description of an expression's syntactic category and semantic type.

Again, I will describe the behavior of an expression in English---what it can combine with, and what it makes as a result---and again, I want you to:

- say what its syntactic category is in "parentheses" notation;
- say what its syntactic category is in "tree" notation;
- say what its semantic type is, assuming the category-type correspondence discussed in [Syntactic categories](../applicative_cg/syn_types.html) of the previous module.
  As before, you can use either the usual notation or the "tree" notation for semantic types here.

(1) This expression takes a preposition to its left, and then a prepositional-dative ditransitive verb to its right, to form a noun phrase.

(2) This expression combines with a coordinator of verb phrases to its right (e.g., *and*), and then a preposition to its left, to form a sentence.

(3) This expression combines with an expression $X$ to its left, where $X$ is something that takes a coordinator of sentences on its left to form a verb phrase, and together with $X$, it forms a preposition.

### Part 2
(30 points)

English has a syntactic *voice* distinction between *active* verbs and *passive* verbs.
This means that in addition to sentences like (@ex-see-active), where we see the transitive verb *saw*,

(@ex-see-active) Sam saw Frodo.

it is also possible to form sentences like (@ex-see-passive), in which the very same verb has been passivized.

(@ex-see-passive) Frodo was seen.

To analyze sentences with passive verbs in them, let's assume that we have another basic syntactic category:

$$v_{\textit{pass.}}$$

Assume that this basic category is associated with the following semantic type:

$$(e → t)$$

Thus *semantically*, $v_{\textit{pass.}}$ is just like the syntactic category $(np\backslash s)$ of verb phrases.

Further, let's assume that *saw* has the following lexical entry:

$$⟨\textit{saw}, (λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))⟩ ⊢ ((np\backslash s)/np)$$

It takes two semantic arguments, one corresponding to the direct object and one corresponding to the subject, and it gives back $\true$ if the second argument sees the first argument (and it gives back $\false$, otherwise).

To analyze the passive verb *seen*, let's assume that it has the following lexical entry:

$$⟨\textit{seen}, (λx.\{y ∣ \ct{see}(y, x)\} ≠ \varnothing)⟩ ⊢ v_{\textit{pass.}}$$

In words, the interpretation of *seen* is a characteristic function of some set of entities.
Specifically, it is the characteristic function of the set of entities such that the set of things that see them is *not* the empty set.

Provide a lexical entry for the auxiliary verb *was* that allows you to derive the sentence in (@ex-see-passive).
Note that it has the following behavior:
it combines with a passive verb on its right;
then it combines with a noun phrase on its left to form a sentence.
You can use this information to derive both the syntactic category of *was* and its semantic type.
Note that the interpretation you provide for it can be *semantically vacuous*, in the same way that the interpretation for *to* was.

Assume, as before, that Sam is a noun phrase whose interpretation is $\ct{s}$, and that *Frodo* is a noun phrase whose interpretation is $\ct{f}$.
Provide a derivation of the sentence in (@ex-see-active).
Use your lexical entry for *was* to provide a derivation for the sentence in (@ex-see-passive).
Do the meanings you obtain for the two sentences help explain the fact that (@ex-see-active) *entails* (@ex-see-passive)?

### Part 3
(30 points)

Consider the following sentence, which features an adjective in predicate position.

(@ex-fast) Frodo is fast.

Assume that there is a new basic category for adjective phrases---call it $ap$---which is the syntactic category of the adjective *fast*.

What semantic type do you think this category should be associated with?
Keep in mind that this semantic type doesn't have to be $e$ or $t$---it can be something more complex!

What syntactic category should the copula *is* have?
Given this syntactic category, what is the semantic type of *is*?

(Please justify your answers.)
